stops.name: Yekaterinoslav, the Fadeyev house, on the night of the cholera
stops.campa: In the house of the Fadeyevs on the Dnieper, while the cholera walks the streets and empties the churches, a daughter is born to Helena Andreyevna and Captain Peter von Hahn. The mother, herself half-dead of the plague, cannot rise; the priest circling the font trails his robe into a candle and sets the vestments alight, and the infant in the water is passed through fire on her first day. The nurses read it at once as an omen: this child will pass her whole life through burnings and be scorched by none of them. She is baptised Helena Petrovna, and the century has met its Sphinx.

stops.name: Saratov, the subterranean corridors and the invisible playmates
stops.campa: The wild girl builds a tower of broken chairs beneath a barred window in the cellar-corridors of the governor's house, and there she is never alone. A troupe of playmates no adult can see keeps her company; her favourite is a small hunchback who leads her into endless mischief. She walks and talks in her sleep, and swears that eyes glare at her out of the furniture and the walls. Above them all stands a majestic Hindu in a white turban whom she calls her Protector, watching over the barred window. The servants cross themselves; the family calls it nerves. She knows it is not.

stops.name: Tiflis, the betrothal to the vice-governor
stops.campa: At the house of her aunt Yekaterina de Witte in Tiflis, seventeen and untamed, Helena is betrothed to Nikifor Blavatsky, a state official three times her age soon to be vice-governor of Erevan. She has boasted she could no more marry the old man than an old crow, and to spite a governess who told her no man would have her, she now accepts him. But the vow she makes is inward and against him: he shall never be a husband to her. The trap of the marriage closes even as she signs herself into it, and she is already planning the flight.

stops.name: Djelal-Oghlu, the marriage fled
stops.campa: Married on the seventh of July in the shadow of the Erevan mountains, she keeps her vow: the marriage is never consummated. Within weeks she is on horseback and gone, over the passes toward the coast, servants scandalised and family shamed behind her. She reaches the Black Sea, bribes her way onto an English sailing-bark bound for Constantinople, and slips out of the whole Russian world at eighteen. The runaway bride becomes, in a single flight, the wanderer she will be for the rest of her life. No governor, no husband, no border will hold her again.

stops.name: Constantinople, the first freedom
stops.campa: In Constantinople the escaped bride finds her feet. She falls in with Countess Kisselev and a circus-rider's world of adventurers, and by her own account rides bareback in the ring for money when the purse runs thin. From here she moves through Greece, Egypt and the Levant with the Countess, a girl of eighteen loose in the East with no chaperone and no plan but forward. The Ottoman capital is the hinge: behind it lies the Russia she fled, ahead the decades of wandering. She has become no one's, and therefore free to become anyone's pupil.

stops.name: London, Hyde Park: the Master Morya in the flesh
stops.campa: On her twentieth birthday, among the crowds of the Great Exhibition, Helena sees walking in the flesh the tall Hindu of her childhood dreams: the Protector of the barred window, come to London with a delegation of Indian princes. She nearly rushes to him; he stops her with a glance, then bids her meet him in Hyde Park. There, seated beside her, Master Morya tells her of the work for which she was born: he needs her cooperation for a task before her, and she must spend three years in Tibet to prepare. She gives her word. The mission of her life is sealed on a park bench.
stops.quote: I saw Master in my visions ever since my childhood... He ordered me to meet Him in Hyde Park.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Blavatsky, letter to A. P. Sinnett (Sinnett, The Letters of H. P. Blavatsky to A. P. Sinnett)

stops.name: New Orleans and the voodoo of the bayous
stops.campa: Under the Master's charge to wander before she is ready, she crosses to the Americas and comes down into New Orleans, drawn to the voodoo of the Black congregations and the sorcery of the swamps. She studies the rites at close hand, hungry for any door into the hidden powers, until, she will say, the Master warns her in a dream of the dark forces she is playing with, and she breaks off and flees the city. The lesson stays: the phenomena are real, but not all hands that raise them are clean. She turns her face toward the deeper South.

stops.name: The Andes and the ruins of Peru
stops.campa: Through Mexico and Central America and down the Pacific coast she rides to Peru, into the dead cities of a vanished race. Among the Andean ruins she reads the signs of a civilisation older and wiser than the conquerors who broke it, and gathers proofs, she will insist, of the single archaic wisdom that once lit every continent before the Flood of history drowned it. The stones of the Incas speak to her of Atlantis and of ages lost. What she carries away is not gold but a thesis: that all the world's temples are shards of one broken lamp.

stops.name: Darjeeling, the border barred
stops.campa: Sent back from the New World toward the East, she comes at last to the roof of the world and tries the door. At the Darjeeling frontier the British turn her back; the way into forbidden Tibet is shut to a lone European woman, and the guardians of the passes do not yet open. She is not ready, and the mountains know it. She withdraws, wanders on through India and beyond, biding the years until the summons comes and the road that no map shows will finally lie open before her feet. The three years the Master named have not yet begun.

stops.name: Kashmir, into Tibet with the Tartar shaman
stops.campa: This time the door opens. Guided by a Tartar shaman who is hurrying home to his own country, disguised and travelling rough through Kashmir and Ladakh, she crosses at last into Little Tibet. On the road the shaman lays her flat with a fever and, by a rite over a lake and a mirror of polished metal, calls up the living image of his own village a thousand miles away for her to see. She has entered the closed land at the feet of the hidden Brotherhood, and the country of the Masters receives her as one long expected.

stops.name: Mentana, five wounds for Garibaldi
stops.campa: Between the Tibetan sojourns she turns up on a battlefield. At Mentana, where Garibaldi's redshirts break against the papal and French rifles, she stands among the volunteers and is cut down: a ball in the shoulder, a shattered arm, a broken leg, and left for dead among the corpses until she is dragged out alive. She keeps the scars and shows them for the rest of her life as proof she was there. The woman of the astral planes bleeds red on the road to Rome; the seer is also a soldier, and both wounds are true in this telling.

stops.name: Shigatse, the ashram of the Masters near Tashilhunpo
stops.campa: Beyond the Himalaya, in the valley of Shigatse under the golden roofs of Tashilhunpo, she comes to rest at last in the house of Master Koot Hoomi, near the seat of the Panchen Lama. Here dwell the Mahatmas: Morya and Koot Hoomi, Kashmiris of the Punjab, adepts of the Gelugpa way who have kept the archaic wisdom alive while the outer world forgot it. She lives at their feet, learns the discipline of the astral senses, and studies the Book of Dzyan, the oldest book on earth, whose verses she will one day give to the West. This is the hidden heart of the whole journey.
